terms: Motif
A recurring image, sound, or idea within or across texts.
Theme
An abstract concern that organises a work's meaning.
Preoccupation
A persistent concern that recurs across an author's writing.
Style signature
Distinctive stylistic features marking an author's writing.
Development
How an author's themes and techniques change across the oeuvre.
Mature work
The phase of an author's writing in which characteristic concerns crystallise.
Influence
The shaping pressure of earlier writers on a later writer's work.
Legacy
An author's lasting impact on subsequent literature.
Tradition
T S Eliot's idea of the living continuity between past and present writing.
Belated
Harold Bloom's term for the latecomer poet wrestling with predecessors.
Misreading
Bloom's idea that strong writers creatively misread their precursors.
Reception
How readers across time have understood and valued a writer.
Biographical criticism
Reading a text in light of the author's life and experiences.
Oeuvre
An author's complete body of work.
Intentional fallacy
Wimsatt and Beardsley's warning against equating meaning with author intent.
Recurring motif
An image or idea that appears repeatedly across an author's work.
Author function
Foucault's concept of authorship as a discursive role rather than a person.
Death of the author
Roland Barthes's essay arguing meaning resides in the reader, not the author.
Comparative study
Analysis of two or more texts to illuminate similarities and differences.
Thematic parallel
A theme shared by multiple texts, providing the axis of comparison.
Point of comparison
A specific angle or question used to align texts for analysis.
Contrast
A meaningful difference between texts that sharpens understanding.
Convergence
Points at which different texts arrive at similar insights.
Divergence
Where similar themes are treated in opposing ways.
Line of inquiry
A precise question that guides the HL Essay's argument.
Thesis
The essay's central claim, sustained throughout the writing.
Evidence selection
Choosing quotations that best support the argument; quality over quantity.
Critical context
Theoretical or scholarly framing brought into the essay.
Conclusion
The synthesis that ties analysis to the line of inquiry.
Word limit
The HL Essay must be 1200-1500 words.
Cross-cultural comparison
Analysis of texts from different cultural traditions.
Form-specific feature
An effect particular to a genre (e.g. line break in poetry).
World literature
Goethe's term for literature circulating beyond national borders.
Translation
The recreation of a text in another language, always an act of interpretation.
Cultural lens
A specific cultural framework used to read a text.
Universal vs particular
The tension between local specificity and broader human resonance.
Orientalism
Edward Said's critique of Western representations of the East as exotic Other.
Subaltern
Gayatri Spivak's term for those denied a voice within hegemonic discourse.
Hybridity
Homi Bhabha's concept of cultural mixing in colonial encounter.
Psychoanalytic criticism
Reading texts through Freudian or Lacanian frames of desire and unconscious.
Uncanny
Freud's das Unheimliche — the strangely familiar that disturbs.
Mimicry
Bhabha's term for the colonised subject's partial imitation of the coloniser.
Marxist criticism
Reading literature in terms of class, ideology and material conditions.
Base and superstructure
Marx's distinction between economic foundation and cultural forms.
Ideology
The system of ideas that naturalises a social order.
Feminist criticism
Analysis of how texts represent and shape gender.
Gynocriticism
Elaine Showalter's term for the study of women writers and female literary traditions.
Ecriture feminine
Helene Cixous's call for a writing rooted in the female body and difference.
Close reading
Detailed analysis of a passage's language, structure and devices.
Formalism
A critical approach focused on form, structure and literariness.
New Criticism
Mid-20th-century US movement emphasising the autonomous text and ambiguity.
PEEL
Point, Evidence, Explain, Link — an essay paragraph structure.
PETER
Point, Evidence, Technique, Explanation, Relevance — analytic paragraph structure.
Ambiguity
William Empson's term for the productive multiplicity of meaning in literature.
Postcolonialism
A critical approach examining the cultural legacy of colonial rule.
Orientalism
Said's critique of Western constructions of the East.
Subaltern
Spivak's term for those excluded from dominant discourse.
Hybridity
Bhabha's concept of cultural mixing in colonial contact zones.
Negritude
The Francophone Black literary movement asserting African cultural value.
Writing back
Postcolonial reworking of canonical European texts.
Frankfurt School
Group of Marxist thinkers including Adorno, Horkheimer, Benjamin and Marcuse.
Culture industry
Adorno and Horkheimer's term for mass-produced culture that reinforces capitalism.
Aura
Walter Benjamin's term for the unique presence of an original artwork.
Ideology
The system of ideas that naturalises social arrangements.
Commodity fetishism
Marx's term for the way commodities mask social relations of production.
Hegemony
Gramsci's term for the consent-based dominance of a ruling group.
Feminism
Movement and theory asserting the political, social and economic equality of women.
Gynocriticism
Showalter's study of women's writing as a distinct tradition.
Performativity
Judith Butler's theory that gender is enacted rather than essential.
Patriarchy
A social system in which men hold primary power.
Female gothic
Gothic fiction by women foregrounding women's confinement and anxiety.
Madwoman in the attic
Gilbert and Gubar's image of Victorian women writers' suppressed creative anger.
Bildungsroman
Coming-of-age narrative tracing moral and psychological growth; Goethe's Wilhelm Meister 1796 set the template; Joyce's Portrait of the Artist a modern instance.
Epistolary novel
Narrative told through letters or documents; Samuel Richardson's Pamela 1740 and Mary Shelley's Frankenstein 1818 use this form.
Free indirect discourse
Third-person narration coloured by a character's voice without quotation marks; pioneered by Jane Austen in Emma 1815.
Magic realism
Fusion of realistic settings with matter-of-fact magical elements; Gabriel Garcia Marquez's One Hundred Years of Solitude 1967 is the canonical example.
Novel of manners
Genre satirising social customs of a defined class; Austen's Pride and Prejudice 1813 and Edith Wharton's Age of Innocence 1920 are paradigms.
Unreliable narrator
Wayne Booth's 1961 term for narrators whose account the reader must distrust; Nabokov's Humbert Humbert in Lolita 1955 typifies it.

Allusion
Indirect reference to another text or event; Eliot's Waste Land notes 1922 list allusions ranging from Dante to Buddhist scripture.
Bakhtin's dialogism
Mikhail Bakhtin's Discourse in the Novel 1934-35: language is always doubly oriented to others' utterances.
Bloom's anxiety of influence
Harold Bloom's 1973 study describes strong poets misreading precursors; six revisionary ratios.
Genette's transtextuality
Palimpsests 1982 distinguishes intertextuality, paratext, metatextuality, hypertextuality and architextuality.
Kristeva's intertextuality
Julia Kristeva coined intertextualite in 1966 essay on Bakhtin; every text is a mosaic of quotations.
Rhys's Wide Sargasso Sea 1966
Jean Rhys's prequel to Jane Eyre rewrites Bertha Mason's Caribbean story; canonical post-colonial intertext.
Affective fallacy
Companion 1949 essay against judging literature by emotional effects on readers; both essays in The Verbal Icon 1954.
Defamiliarisation
Shklovsky's 1917 ostranenie concept: art makes the familiar strange to renew perception; example from Tolstoy's Kholstomer.
Fabula and syuzhet
Distinction between raw story material (fabula) and its plotted arrangement (syuzhet); foundational for narratology.
Intentional fallacy
Wimsatt and Beardsley's 1946 essay rejecting reliance on authorial intention in evaluating a poem's meaning.
New Criticism
1940s-50s Anglo-American school led by Cleanth Brooks, John Crowe Ransom and Robert Penn Warren; close reading of the verbal icon.
Russian Formalism
1915-30 movement; OPOYAZ in Petrograd and Moscow Linguistic Circle; Shklovsky, Eikhenbaum, Tomashevsky and Tynyanov.

Allusion
An indirect reference to another text, figure or event.
Parody
Comic imitation of another work that exaggerates its features.
Pastiche
Imitation that pays homage without mockery.
Quotation
Direct citation of another text, marked or unmarked.
Influence
Harold Bloom's term for the inescapable debt of writers to predecessors.
Anxiety of influence
Bloom's theory that strong writers struggle against the shadow of precursors.
Archetype
A recurring symbol, character or pattern across literature (Frye, Jung).
Myth criticism
Northrop Frye's approach grouping literature into seasonal mythoi: comedy, romance, tragedy, irony.
Adaptation
Transposing a text into a new medium or genre.
Hypertext
A text derived from a prior text (hypotext) through transformation or imitation.
Transposition
Genette's term for serious transformation, e.g. Joyce's Ulysses from the Odyssey.
Quest narrative
Archetypal journey involving departure, trial and return.
Genre
A category of text defined by shared formal and thematic conventions.
Generic hybridity
The mixing of two or more genres within a single text.
Convention
A recurring feature that signals genre to readers.
Subversion
Undermining or rewriting a genre's conventions.
Horizon of expectations
Jauss's term for the prior assumptions a reader brings to a text.
Metafiction
Fiction that draws attention to its own status as fiction.
Novel
An extended prose narrative, typically dealing with character and society.
Bildungsroman
A novel of formation, tracing a protagonist's moral and psychological growth.
Epistolary novel
A novel told through letters or other documents.
Gothic novel
A subgenre featuring castles, ruins, terror and the supernatural.
Magical realism
Realist narrative with embedded magical elements treated as ordinary.
Picaresque
Episodic novel following a roguish protagonist through adventures.
Sonnet
A 14-line poem in iambic pentameter, typically with a volta.
Volta
The 'turn' in a sonnet's argument, often between octave and sestet.
Ode
A formal lyric address, often of praise or meditation.
Free verse
Poetry without regular metre or rhyme, governed by cadence.
Iambic pentameter
A line of five iambs (unstressed-stressed pairs).
Enjambment
Continuation of a sentence beyond a line break.
Tragedy
A serious drama ending in catastrophe, typically involving a flawed protagonist.
Hamartia
Aristotle's term for the tragic protagonist's flaw or error.
Catharsis
Aristotle's purging of pity and fear through tragedy.
Comedy
A drama with a happy ending, often involving reconciliation and marriage.
History play
Drama based on historical events, especially Shakespeare's English kings.
Creative non-fiction
Prose that applies literary craft to factual material.
Intertextuality
Julia Kristeva's concept that texts derive meaning through relationships with other texts.
Allusion
A brief, often indirect reference to another text, event or figure.
Dialogism
Bakhtin's notion that texts contain multiple voices in dialogue.
Hypotext
An earlier text upon which a later text (hypertext) is built (Genette).
Palimpsest
A text written over an earlier one, where traces of the original remain visible.
Pastiche
An imitation of another work's style, often as homage rather than mockery.
Syntax
The arrangement of words to form sentences and the rhythmic effect this creates.
Tone
The writer's attitude toward subject and audience, conveyed through language choices.
Imagery
Sensory language that evokes sight, sound, taste, touch or smell.
Connotation
The implied or associated meaning of a word beyond its denotation.
Free indirect discourse
A blend of third-person narration and character thought, popularised by Austen and Flaubert.
Register
The level of formality or informality in language, shaped by context and audience.
Narrative voice
The persona through which a story is told; may be first person, third person limited, or omniscient.
Focalisation
Gerard Genette's term for the perspective through which narrative information is filtered.
Reader response
Wolfgang Iser's theory that meaning emerges through the reader's active engagement with textual gaps.
Style
The distinctive manner of expression, including diction, syntax, and rhythm.
Diction
The author's choice of words and their connotations.
Implied reader
The hypothetical reader that the text seems to address and shape.
Analepsis
Genette's term for flashback — a return to an earlier event.
Prolepsis
Genette's term for flash-forward or foreshadowing.
In medias res
Beginning a narrative in the middle of the action.
Story vs discourse
Story is the chronological events; discourse is the order in which they are told.
Duration
The relation between the time events take in the story and the space they occupy in the text.
Frequency
How often an event is narrated relative to how often it occurs.
Zeitgeist
The defining spirit or mood of a particular period of history.
Cultural moment
The intersection of political, social, and artistic forces at a specific time.
Reception history
How a text has been read and valued by successive audiences.
Canon
The body of texts traditionally regarded as authoritative within a literary tradition.
Periodisation
Dividing literary history into periods such as Romantic, Modernist, Postmodern.
Print culture
The historical conditions of book production and circulation.
Setting
The time, place and social environment in which a text is set.
Psychogeography
The study of how geographical environments shape emotional and psychological states.
Historical context
The political, social and cultural moment of a work's composition.
Chronotope
Bakhtin's term for the time-space configuration of a genre.
Local colour
Detailed depiction of regional customs, dialect and landscape.
Sense of place
The distinct character and emotional resonance attached to a particular location.
